vignette: John, a 20-year-old African American doctor, had recently returned from his first tour of duty in combat. He presented with severe symptoms consistent with PTSD, reflected by a PCL-5 score of 63. John's narrative unfolded as a series of fragmented and disorienting experiences that significantly impacted his daily life and sense of self. John vividly recalled the traumatic event during which he was severely injured while treating casualties under intense gunfire. He had been hit by shrapnel, leaving him breathless and struggling to continue his duties amidst sudden bursts of silence and ongoing violence. The memory of this incident was not cohesive; instead, it came in disconnected pieces that did not fit together, with significant gaps in his recollection. In the aftermath of his injury, John found himself increasingly vigilant about his surroundings. He had come to believe that he needed to be constantly on guard to avoid another similar traumatic event. This hypervigilance led him to feel like a stranger to himself; he no longer recognized the person who once felt secure and confident in both his abilities as a doctor and his understanding of the world around him. John's sense of identity loss was further exacerbated by his memory gaps and fragmented recollections. He pushed away thoughts of the event whenever they began to surface, unable to bear fully confronting what had happened. This avoidance only reinforced his negative appraisals that his beliefs about the world were shattered beyond repair. The more he tried to block out these memories, the more intense his hypervigilance became. At work, John's triggers often manifested in ways that affected his ability to function as a doctor. During quiet moments between patients or while alone in the hospital corridors, the sudden silence would trigger flashbacks of the battlefield. These auditory triggers not only brought back fragmented memories but also intensified his hypervigilance and sense of self-doubt. He became increasingly anxious about returning to the same places where he used to feel safe and competent. His hypervigilance extended beyond work into his personal life, making it difficult for him to engage in social activities or maintain close relationships. John's heightened state of alertness often made him irritable and distant from others. He found himself isolating more frequently, believing that nobody could understand the trauma he had experienced. John's memory gaps and fragmented recollections further exacerbated his negative appraisals about identity loss and shattered beliefs. He struggled to piece together a coherent narrative of what happened during his deployment, which only deepened his feelings of uncertainty and confusion. The more he pushed away these memories, the more they resurfaced in unexpected ways, often triggered by seemingly mundane events that mirrored aspects of the traumatic experience. The cycle tightened as John's hypervigilance led him to avoid situations where he might encounter silence or violence, making it difficult for him to engage fully with his work and personal life. His negative appraisals reinforced his memory gaps, creating a self-perpetuating loop of distress. Finally, the cumulative strain on both his professional and personal life brought John to seek help. He was most afraid that he would never feel like himself again and was desperately hoping for relief from the relentless cycle of fear and confusion that had taken over his life. Through therapy, he hoped to regain a sense of self and find a way to integrate his traumatic experiences without losing who he truly is.
